## Question and audience

This project will investigate the question: How well can NBA players' regular-season performance statistics predict their annual salaries from 2010 through 2025? The intended audience includes basketball fans, sports analysts, NBA salary analyists, NBA players, and NBA front-office staff who are interested in how much player performance relates to compensation. These relationships are important because they could help explain which statistics are associated with higher salaries and how accurately salary can be predicted from performance data.

The response variable is annual salary (Salary). Important candidate predictors include points per game (PTS), assists (AST), rebounds (TRB), minutes played per game (MP), age (Age), games played (G), steals (STL), and blocks (BLK). Season (Year) will also be considered because salary levels and league conditions change over time.



## Data

The data come from the public GitHub repository NBA Salary Prediction, which includes the file NBA Player Stats and Salaries_2010-2025.csv. The dataset contains 7,298 rows and 31 variables from 2010–2025. The observational unit is a player-season-team record. The response is annual salary in dollars, and the candidate predictors are regular-season statistics, player age, and season

The repository describes combining and cleaning player statistics and salary information from sources that include Basketball Reference and other Basketball databases. The data contain public professional sports information and does not appear to require or show private personal information. Potential limitations not in the dataset include  factors such as contract length, injuries, experience, position, foul history, team finances, and contract timing. Also, players who changed teams within a season may also have more than one row, so the unit of observation and any duplicate player-season records will need to be considered during data cleaning.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)

nba <- read_csv("NBA Player Stats and Salaries_2010-2025.csv")

tibble(
  observations = nrow(nba),
  variables = ncol(nba),
  unique_players = n_distinct(nba$Player),
  seasons = n_distinct(nba$Year),
  missing_salary = sum(is.na(nba$Salary)),
  missing_points = sum(is.na(nba$PTS))
)

names(nba)

```

## Baseline model

**Name and justify one simple starting model.**
A reasonable starting model is a multiple linear regression of log salary on points per game and season:

[
\log(\text{Salary}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1(\text{PTS}) + \text{season effects} + \varepsilon.
]

The logarithmic transformation is appropriate as a starting point because salaries are strongly right-skewed. Including season effects helps account for differences in salary levels across years, while points per game provides a simple measure of offensive performance.


```{r}
# Fit the baseline and display only the output needed below.
baseline_model <- lm(log(Salary) ~ PTS + factor(Year), data = nba)

pts_estimate <- coef(baseline_model)["PTS"]
pts_interval <- confint(baseline_model)["PTS", ]

tibble(
  term = "Points per game",
  estimated_percent_difference = 100 * (exp(pts_estimate) - 1),
  lower_95_percent = 100 * (exp(pts_interval[1]) - 1),
  upper_95_percent = 100 * (exp(pts_interval[2]) - 1)
)
```

**Interpret one important coefficient, contrast, or prediction in context. Include direction, magnitude, units or scale, and uncertainty. Then identify one specific limitation, unexplained pattern, or opportunity for improvement.**
In the baseline model fitted to the supplied dataset, one additional point per game is associated with approximately 15% higher annual salary, holding season constant. The estimated 95% confidence interval is approximately 14.5% to 15.5%. This describes an average association in the fitted model, not a guaranteed salary increase for an individual player. One limitation is that points per game alone cannot capture other important factors, such as assists, rebounds, defensive contributions, injuries, or contract terms. The model's assumptions and predictive performance will need further evaluation.
